screens.title: EtherChannel (Link Aggregation) Configuration
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll learn how to combine multiple Ethernet links into a single logical interface so you can both increase effective bandwidth and gain resilient failover. EtherChannel bundles present a single Port-channel to the network while using multiple physical links underneath. That means traffic can be balanced across members, and if one physical cable fails, the logical link stays up and carries traffic on remaining links. We'll also compare the negotiation approaches: the vendor-proprietary Port Aggregation Protocol and the standards-based Link Aggregation Control Protocol, plus the static or "on" mode that skips negotiation. You will see a practical configuration pattern used on Catalyst switches: prepare interfaces so they match, assign them to a channel-group, and apply trunk or access settings to the Port-channel. Finally, you will practice verification and troubleshooting steps like checking EtherChannel summary and per-interface EtherChannel status. By the end you'll be able to choose a negotiation mode, configure an EtherChannel, and diagnose common mismatches. Consider how this affects spanning tree behavior and traffic distribution as you proceed.

screens.title: What is EtherChannel and why use it?
screens.narratorSegment: EtherChannel is a link aggregation technique that groups multiple physical Ethernet interfaces into a single logical Port-channel. The immediate benefit is increased aggregate bandwidth: for example, combining four one-gigabit links yields a logical four-gigabit connection. Equally important is redundancy. If one member link fails, the Port-channel remains active and traffic automatically moves to remaining members. This behavior differs from simple redundant links that rely on Spanning Tree Protocol to block paths; EtherChannel keeps all physical links usable, avoiding wasted capacity. A practical example is connecting an access-layer switch to a distribution switch with four Gigabit links. Instead of one active and three blocked links by spanning tree, you get a single Port-channel carrying traffic across four physical wires, with faster recovery when a cable or NIC fails. Common misconceptions include thinking EtherChannel multiplies single-flow throughput; in reality, load balancing pins a single conversation to a member link, so a single TCP flow may not exceed one member's capacity. However, many flows across different hosts will benefit from the aggregated capacity. Think of EtherChannel as logical trunking that preserves link redundancy while enabling better use of physical ports.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › What is EtherChannel?
Definition & Benefits

EtherChannel creates a logical Port-channel from multiple physical Ethernet links. Benefits include increased aggregate bandwidth and link redundancy with automatic failover at Layer 2.

Increased effective bandwidth: combine link capacities.
Redundancy: single physical failure doesn’t bring down the Port-channel.
Better utilization than STP blocking because all links carry traffic.
Concrete Example
Scenario
Four Gigabit links between switches

Aggregate to an approximate 4 Gbps logical link while retaining seamless failover if a cable fails.

Misconception
Single-flow speed

A single conversation typically uses one member link determined by load-balance. EtherChannel increases overall capacity across multiple flows, not necessarily single-flow bandwidth.

Key Takeaway

EtherChannel gives you higher total throughput and graceful degradation; design expectations around how traffic distributes across member links.

screens.title: PAgP, LACP, and Static (on) Modes
screens.narratorSegment: EtherChannel can be created using three approaches: PAgP, LACP, or static on. PAgP is Cisco proprietary and uses desirable and auto modes. Desirable actively negotiates while auto waits; one side must be desirable for a bundle to form. LACP is the standards-based IEEE approach and uses active and passive modes with parallel logic: at least one active side required. Choose LACP when you need interoperability with non-Cisco devices. Static on forces member interfaces into a bundle without negotiation; this is brittle because it performs no protocol-level checks and can lead to misconfigured bundles if the peer is not configured identically. A common mistake is mixing negotiation types—if one switch uses LACP and the other uses PAgP, negotiation will fail and members will not form a Port-channel. Another pitfall is having both sides passive or both sides auto; without an active initiator, no negotiation takes place. In practice use LACP for multi-vendor environments and PAgP only when both ends are Cisco and legacy behavior is required. Reserve static on for tightly controlled environments where you can ensure complete manual consistency. PAgP, LACP, and Static (on) Modes means prefer lacp for interoperability, pagp for cisco-only legacy scenarios, and avoid static on unless you can guarantee identical manual configuration on both ends.. In practical terms, negotiation behaviors and interoperability constraints. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Negotiation Modes
Protocol comparison
LACP
Active / Passive modes. Standard 802.3ad, multi-vendor compatible.
PAgP
Desirable / Auto. Cisco-proprietary; only works with Cisco peers.
Static (on)
No negotiation. Requires identical manual config; prone to error.
Interoperability tip

If peers use different protocols, the EtherChannel will not form. Avoid mixing LACP with PAgP and ensure at least one side actively initiates negotiation for protocol-based setups.

Common Mistakes
  • Both sides passive or both sides auto — no negotiation occurs.
  • Mixing LACP and PAgP across a link — negotiation fails.
  • Using static on without ensuring identical member configs — can cause traffic blackholing.
Warning

Static on has no negotiation checks. Use it only when you control both ends and need to force a bundle.

screens.title: Configuring EtherChannel — Prechecks and steps
screens.narratorSegment: Successful EtherChannel configuration begins with careful preparation. First, identify candidate interfaces and ensure they share identical settings: speed, duplex, switchport mode, trunk encapsulation, allowed VLANs, and STP port type. If any parameter differs, that interface will refuse to join the Port-channel. Second, configure the physical interfaces consistently—for example set trunk mode and allowed VLANs—then assign them to the same channel-group number with the desired negotiation mode. This creates a Port-channel logical interface. Third, apply trunking or IP addressing to the Port-channel interface rather than the member interfaces; the Port-channel is the proper locus for higher-level settings and is inherited by members. Finally, set a global load-balancing policy if needed and verify. A common procedural error is applying trunk allowed VLANs only to physical ports and not to the Port-channel, which can cause inconsistent behavior. A practical checklist: confirm VLAN existence, match interface parameters, issue channel-group with a consistent mode, configure Port-channel properties, and run verification commands. These steps ensure the logical bundle forms predictably and forwards traffic as intended. Configuring EtherChannel — Prechecks and steps means match interface settings, add to channel-group with correct mode, configure the port-channel, and verify bundle health with show commands.. In practical terms, prepare member interfaces, create channel-group, and apply port-channel settings. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Configuring LACP EtherChannel — Switch-A (active)
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a typical LACP configuration on one side of the link. On Switch-A you prepare Gigabit interfaces, set trunk encapsulation, specify allowed VLANs, and group the interfaces with LACP active mode. This sequence ensures the switch actively negotiates with its peer. After you issue the channel-group command the Port-channel logical interface is created, and best practice is to apply trunking and VLAN settings to that Port-channel so the bundle inherits consistent behavior. In the lab you will see that if Switch-A is active and Switch-B is passive, LACP negotiation completes and both member ports become active members. A common mistake is configuring channel-group on member ports but forgetting to configure the Port-channel with trunk allowed VLANs; this leads to inconsistent VLAN forwarding. When you type these commands, watch for command output that confirms the channel-group membership and the LACP negotiation state. After configuration, verify with show etherchannel summary to confirm the bundle is up and member ports are listed as active. screens.title: Load Balancing in EtherChannel
screens.narratorSegment: Load balancing decides which physical member carries a frame inside a Port-channel. Common algorithms use source MAC, destination MAC, source IP, destination IP, or combinations like source-destination IP. For example, with a source-MAC algorithm, all traffic from a host keeps using the same physical link because the source address hashes to a particular member. This guarantees in-order delivery for that host's flows but risks uneven utilization when one host sends most traffic. Using source-destination IP hashing increases distribution granularity by including both endpoints, which tends to spread traffic across more members when many hosts communicate. Remember that load balancing is configured globally on the switch, not per-Port-channel, so choose a method aligned with your traffic patterns. A common mistake is leaving the default method without considering whether most traffic is many small flows or a few heavy flows. Observe traffic behavior after changing the algorithm to ensure it improves distribution. Finally, note that no algorithm perfectly balances every scenario; use monitoring and adjust when you discover skewed patterns. Load Balancing in EtherChannel means select a load-balancing algorithm that matches traffic patterns; configure it globally to influence how flows map to member links.. In practical terms, how traffic maps to member links and why it matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Troubleshooting Common EtherChannel Issues
screens.narratorSegment: Troubleshooting EtherChannel problems is a process of elimination. Start by examining show etherchannel summary to see whether the Port-channel appears and which ports are members. If member ports are missing, check per-interface etherchannel status to view negotiation messages and error hints. The most frequent root causes are mismatched speed or duplex, inconsistent switchport modes, different trunk encapsulation, unequal allowed VLAN lists, and native VLAN mismatches. Another frequent error is mismatched negotiation: one side configured for LACP while the other uses PAgP, or one side in on mode while the other is negotiating. Resolve by restoring symmetry: set identical speed/duplex, match trunk encapsulation and allowed VLANs, and align negotiation modes. If the Port-channel forms but only one physical link forwards traffic excessively, review the load-balancing algorithm and traffic patterns; a single heavy source will remain on one member with some algorithms. Use show interfaces to check physical errors and monitor counters to confirm packet distribution. Systematic verification and small corrective steps avoid configuration churn and reduce downtime. screens.title: Best Practices and Common Mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: Adopt a few consistent best practices to reduce EtherChannel operational risk. Always use a protocol such as LACP when interoperability or automatic verification matters. Reserve static on for tightly controlled environments where you can guarantee identical configurations on both ends. Keep member interface configurations identical and avoid configuring higher-level settings only on members—apply trunking and VLAN lists to the Port-channel. Choose a global load-balancing algorithm based on traffic patterns; many data-center designs prefer source-destination IP hashing to spread flows across multiple links. Monitor bundle health with regular show commands and check for error counters on physical interfaces. Common mistakes to avoid: mixing negotiation protocols across the link, mismatched native VLANs, unequal trunk allowed-vlan lists, and expecting all single flows to exceed a member link's speed. If you expect single-flow acceleration, consider technologies like EtherChannel combined with flow-level load balancers or multithreaded transports at higher layers. Plan changes carefully and verify each step to prevent service disruption. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll learn how to combine multiple Ethernet links into a single logical interface so you can both increase effective bandwidth and gain resilient failover. EtherChannel bundles present a single Port-channel to the network while using multiple physical links underneath. That means traffic can be balanced across members, and if one physical cable fails, the logical link stays up and carries traffic on remaining links. We'll also compare the negotiation approaches: the vendor-proprietary Port Aggregation Protocol and the standards-based Link Aggregation Control Protocol, plus the static or "on" mode that skips negotiation. You will see a practical configuration pattern used on Catalyst switches: prepare interfaces so they match, assign them to a channel-group, and apply trunk or access settings to the Port-channel. Finally, you will practice verification and troubleshooting steps like checking EtherChannel summary and per-interface EtherChannel status. By the end you'll be able to choose a negotiation mode, configure an EtherChannel, and diagnose common mismatches. Consider how this affects spanning tree behavior and traffic distribution as you proceed.

These objectives focus your practice and assessment. First, you'll explain why EtherChannel is used: it increases aggregate bandwidth and offers link redundancy without relying on a blocked spanning-tree port to carry traffic. Second, you will distinguish negotiation methods: you'll describe PAgP's Cisco-proprietary desirable/auto modes, LACP's active/passive modes, and the static on mode that requires manual configuration. Third, you will configure EtherChannel on Catalyst switches using a channel-group to create a Port-channel and apply trunk or access settings to the logical interface rather than each member. Fourth, you will choose and set an appropriate load-balancing method and verify the bundle with show commands. Each objective includes a short verification milestone so you can demonstrate competency in lab tasks and troubleshooting scenarios. Together these skills let you design resilient, higher-capacity links and diagnose common formation failures in real networks.

This second objectives slide focuses on hands-on outcomes. You will configure both ends of a bundle so that interfaces match in speed, duplex, trunk settings, and allowed VLANs. You will practice creating a channel-group and verify that the Port-channel inherits the logical settings. In labs, you will configure LACP with one switch in active and the peer in passive, demonstrating a successful negotiation. You will also set load balancing globally and observe how different algorithms affect traffic distribution. Finally, you will diagnose misconfiguration scenarios—mismatched native VLANs, trunk allowed-vlan differences, or mixed negotiation types—and resolve them. These practical milestones prepare you to run the verification commands and interpret status outputs to confirm that all member links are Active and forwarding. Learning Objectives — Practical Skills means configure matching member interfaces, create channel-groups, set port-channel properties, choose load-balancing, and run verification commands.. In practical terms, hands-on configuration and verification targets. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

EtherChannel is a link aggregation technique that groups multiple physical Ethernet interfaces into a single logical Port-channel. The immediate benefit is increased aggregate bandwidth: for example, combining four one-gigabit links yields a logical four-gigabit connection. Equally important is redundancy. If one member link fails, the Port-channel remains active and traffic automatically moves to remaining members. This behavior differs from simple redundant links that rely on Spanning Tree Protocol to block paths; EtherChannel keeps all physical links usable, avoiding wasted capacity. A practical example is connecting an access-layer switch to a distribution switch with four Gigabit links. Instead of one active and three blocked links by spanning tree, you get a single Port-channel carrying traffic across four physical wires, with faster recovery when a cable or NIC fails. Common misconceptions include thinking EtherChannel multiplies single-flow throughput; in reality, load balancing pins a single conversation to a member link, so a single TCP flow may not exceed one member's capacity. However, many flows across different hosts will benefit from the aggregated capacity. Think of EtherChannel as logical trunking that preserves link redundancy while enabling better use of physical ports.

EtherChannel can be created using three approaches: PAgP, LACP, or static on. PAgP is Cisco proprietary and uses desirable and auto modes. Desirable actively negotiates while auto waits; one side must be desirable for a bundle to form. LACP is the standards-based IEEE approach and uses active and passive modes with parallel logic: at least one active side required. Choose LACP when you need interoperability with non-Cisco devices. Static on forces member interfaces into a bundle without negotiation; this is brittle because it performs no protocol-level checks and can lead to misconfigured bundles if the peer is not configured identically. A common mistake is mixing negotiation types—if one switch uses LACP and the other uses PAgP, negotiation will fail and members will not form a Port-channel. Another pitfall is having both sides passive or both sides auto; without an active initiator, no negotiation takes place. In practice use LACP for multi-vendor environments and PAgP only when both ends are Cisco and legacy behavior is required. Reserve static on for tightly controlled environments where you can ensure complete manual consistency. PAgP, LACP, and Static (on) Modes means prefer lacp for interoperability, pagp for cisco-only legacy scenarios, and avoid static on unless you can guarantee identical manual configuration on both ends.. In practical terms, negotiation behaviors and interoperability constraints. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Successful EtherChannel configuration begins with careful preparation. First, identify candidate interfaces and ensure they share identical settings: speed, duplex, switchport mode, trunk encapsulation, allowed VLANs, and STP port type. If any parameter differs, that interface will refuse to join the Port-channel. Second, configure the physical interfaces consistently—for example set trunk mode and allowed VLANs—then assign them to the same channel-group number with the desired negotiation mode. This creates a Port-channel logical interface. Third, apply trunking or IP addressing to the Port-channel interface rather than the member interfaces; the Port-channel is the proper locus for higher-level settings and is inherited by members. Finally, set a global load-balancing policy if needed and verify. A common procedural error is applying trunk allowed VLANs only to physical ports and not to the Port-channel, which can cause inconsistent behavior. A practical checklist: confirm VLAN existence, match interface parameters, issue channel-group with a consistent mode, configure Port-channel properties, and run verification commands. These steps ensure the logical bundle forms predictably and forwards traffic as intended. Configuring EtherChannel — Prechecks and steps means match interface settings, add to channel-group with correct mode, configure the port-channel, and verify bundle health with show commands.. In practical terms, prepare member interfaces, create channel-group, and apply port-channel settings. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk through a typical LACP configuration on one side of the link. On Switch-A you prepare Gigabit interfaces, set trunk encapsulation, specify allowed VLANs, and group the interfaces with LACP active mode. This sequence ensures the switch actively negotiates with its peer. After you issue the channel-group command the Port-channel logical interface is created, and best practice is to apply trunking and VLAN settings to that Port-channel so the bundle inherits consistent behavior. In the lab you will see that if Switch-A is active and Switch-B is passive, LACP negotiation completes and both member ports become active members. A common mistake is configuring channel-group on member ports but forgetting to configure the Port-channel with trunk allowed VLANs; this leads to inconsistent VLAN forwarding. When you type these commands, watch for command output that confirms the channel-group membership and the LACP negotiation state. After configuration, verify with show etherchannel summary to confirm the bundle is up and member ports are listed as active. Configuring LACP EtherChannel — Switch-A (active) means set member interfaces, channel-group in active mode, then configure port-channel trunking so logical settings apply to the bundle.. In practical terms, terminal-style configuration and explanation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

On the peer switch you must mirror the member interface settings and use a compatible LACP mode. If Switch-A is using active mode, Switch-B using passive mode will accept and complete negotiation. The critical item is symmetry: speed, duplex, trunk encapsulation, and allowed VLANs must match. Load balancing decides which physical member carries a frame inside a Port-channel. Common algorithms use source MAC, destination MAC, source IP, destination IP, or combinations like source-destination IP. For example, with a source-MAC algorithm, all traffic from a host keeps using the same physical link because the source address hashes to a particular member. This guarantees in-order delivery for that host's flows but risks uneven utilization when one host sends most traffic. Using source-destination IP hashing increases distribution granularity by including both endpoints, which tends to spread traffic across more members when many hosts communicate. Remember that load balancing is configured globally on the switch, not per-Port-channel, so choose a method aligned with your traffic patterns. A common mistake is leaving the default method without considering whether most traffic is many small flows or a few heavy flows. Observe traffic behavior after changing the algorithm to ensure it improves distribution. Finally, note that no algorithm perfectly balances every scenario; use monitoring and adjust when you discover skewed patterns. Adopt a few consistent best practices to reduce EtherChannel operational risk. Always use a protocol such as LACP when interoperability or automatic verification matters. Reserve static on for tightly controlled environments where you can guarantee identical configurations on both ends. Keep member interface configurations identical and avoid configuring higher-level settings only on members—apply trunking and VLAN lists to the Port-channel. Choose a global load-balancing algorithm based on traffic patterns; many data-center designs prefer source-destination IP hashing to spread flows across multiple links.
